posts.text: So watch and (fingers crossed 🤞🤞😊) enjoy as the crooked MAGA DOJ and Trump’s sketchy lawyers have to explain themselves in court about why their settlement-that’s-called-a-settlement-but-wasn’t-disclosed-to-the-court is not collusive and their behavior not a fraud on the court. Bring popcorn!

One inquiry worth pursuing: was this fund set up as a vehicle to pay a Trump political militia to meddle in November’s elections with intimidation, harassment or even violence against voters at polling places? Inquiring minds want to know.

The pleading requests that the court, via either of two possible channels, reopen the case under its general authority to protect the judicial system from deliberate fraud on the court or wrongful abuse of the court system, a general protection the judiciary has against extraordinary scams like this one.

The corrupt slush fund scheme was for sure a “settlement”;  that’s on the title of the slush fund document, and they even used the caption, title, court and case number of the case from which they had scarpered. So on its face, it’s a “settlement” in the court case.

That’s multiply stinky: from the failure of candor to the court; from dodging the court’s announced “case or controversy” inquiry; and from ducking the court’s powers of approval or disapproval of a settlement (particularly here where the prospect of collusion is so obvious).

Short version: when the court started looking at whether this was a sham “case or controversy” with Trump on both sides, the Trump lawyers (on one side) withdrew their complaint and “settled” with the Trump lawyers on the other side, without telling the court about the “settlement.”

If you hate Trump’s wildly corrupt $1.8 billion “cop-beaters’ slush fund” as much as I do, you’ll enjoy reading this pleading by outraged retired federal judges calling out the “deceit” and “fraud on the court” of the corrupt Trump scheme. 🧵

The Post editorial page has become a creepy sibling to the WSJ’s Polluter Page, when it should fly the moral standard of the paper.
A fading and degraded Washington Post is not an outcome justifiable by financial concerns, particularly not from owners with uncountable wealth.
Are financials a metric? Of course. But other metrics also matter in a democracy that counts on a fearless and independent Fourth Estate.

Bezos BS: “The Post needs to be a profitable enterprise that stands on its own two feet.” 

A great newspaper is a public trust many owners would be proud to support.

It's not just about billionaires paying more in taxes.
 
It's about an America where the people who have the most leave everyone else to pick up their slack.

Only violators of industry’s own standards would pay; money would go back to fund leak repairs; that was too much for them.

Corrupt fossil fuel industry got Senate to gut the methane fee that would have made this happen.
